cards.title: COGS Drives Unit Economics and Valuation
cards.summary: Why COGS accuracy matters for ecommerce operators: it sets the cash left per unit for marketing and R&D and drives gross margin used in valuations.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product can fund its own acquisition and reinvestment, or preparing gross margin figures for investors or lenders.
steps: Take the sale price of a unit. Subtract only the true cost of delivering that unit (materials, direct labor, factory overhead, freight-in, packaging, or for digital: servers, delivery APIs, support and implementation wages depending on model).

The remaining gross profit per unit is the pool available for marketing, R&D and overhead. If gross profit per unit cannot cover customer acquisition cost plus contribution to overhead, the unit is not economically viable at that price.
Recognise that external valuers look at revenue growth and gross margin together; a misclassified cost that understates COGS inflates gross margin and distorts the valuation multiple.
Use the corrected gross margin to decide whether to make more of the same product, reprice, or discontinue and build a new product.
Keep a simple per-SKU gross profit calculation so repricing and promotion decisions are grounded in the same numbers shown to investors.
caveats: Gross margin is not the only valuation input; growth, retention and market matter too.
The source frames this for finance leaders and founders; the application to SKU-level decisions is an adaptation of that principle.

cards.title: Freight-In Versus Freight-Out Classification
cards.summary: Freight-in is COGS but freight-out (shipping to customers) is an operating expense; misclassifying it distorts gross margin.
cards.use_when: Setting up the chart of accounts or reviewing shipping cost treatment for an ecommerce store that ships physical products to customers.
steps: Split freight into two accounts: freight-in (inbound materials, packaging and components to your production or assembly location) and freight-out (outbound shipping to customers).
Record freight-in as part of COGS because it is a cost of acquiring the goods you sell.
Record freight-out as a selling/operating expense, not COGS. Shipping your finished product to a buyer is a distribution and selling activity, not production.
If you offer free shipping and subsidise it, the subsidy sits in operating/selling costs, not COGS — but track it separately so you can see its true margin impact.
Review the split with your accountant before using gross margin as a pricing or valuation signal, because the classification changes the reported margin materially.
caveats: The source states this as a strict accounting rule; treatment can differ under some reporting frameworks, so confirm with your accountant.
This is an accounting classification, not a pricing decision — you can still price shipping into the customer price.

cards.title: CPG vs SaaS Cost Structures and Margin Benchmarks
cards.summary: CPG/manufacturing carries high tangible COGS and 20-40% gross margins; SaaS carries lower labor/server COGS and 70-90% gross margins.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product model to build or expand, or sanity-checking whether your store's gross margin is in a normal range for its category.
steps: For a tangible/CPG product, build COGS from raw materials, direct manufacturing labor, factory overhead (rent, equipment depreciation, maintenance, utilities), freight-in and packaging.
For a software/digital product, build COGS from server or hosting cost, third-party delivery APIs and tools, customer support wages and implementation/onboarding wages.
Compare your gross margin against the source's rule of thumb: roughly 20-40% for CPG/manufacturing and 70-90% for SaaS. The source cites a baby-food manufacturer at about 30% as typical.

When deciding where to build, weigh margin against distribution opportunity: the source notes a CPG product may take a small slice of a very large pie, while SaaS offers higher margin but depends on your skills and idea.
Do not treat the benchmarks as targets; use them to flag whether a cost has been misclassified or a price is structurally too low.
caveats: The 20-40% and 70-90% bands are the source's rule-of-thumb heuristics, not calculated thresholds for any specific store.
A CPG product with strong distribution can win on absolute profit despite low margin.

cards.title: Balance Sheet to P&L Timing for Inventory Versus Services
cards.summary: CPG costs sit on the balance sheet as inventory until sale, while many SaaS costs like wages hit the P&L immediately.
cards.use_when: Forecasting cash and monthly profitability, or explaining to a founder-investor why a stock build-up hurts cash before it hits COGS.
steps: For physical products, capitalise inventory (including freight-in) as an asset on the balance sheet when produced or purchased, then move it to COGS on the P&L only when the item sells.
Understand that building stock consumes cash now and reduces reported profit later — useful when planning seasonal buys or bulk purchasing for cost savings.

For a SaaS/digital product, most COGS (support wages, implementation wages) hits the P&L immediately; only capitalised fixed assets such as owned servers or computers flow from the balance sheet into COGS via depreciation over time.
If you rent server capacity (AWS/Azure), the monthly fee goes straight to COGS rather than being depreciated.
Use this distinction when forecasting: a stock-heavy quarter depresses cash before it depresses profit, while a services-heavy quarter depresses profit immediately.
caveats: The source notes most modern small companies rent rather than own servers; ownership changes the accounting treatment.
Inventory costing methods (e.g. FIFO/weighted average) are not covered here.

cards.title: Customer Success Belongs in Operating Expenses, Not COGS
cards.summary: In SaaS-like models, support and implementation wages are COGS, but customer success teams handling renewals and upsells are a selling function.
cards.use_when: Allocating team costs for a subscription or membership store so that gross margin and retention investment are reported correctly.
steps: Split your delivery organisation into three functions: customer support, customer success and implementation.
Put customer support wages in COGS — they keep the product working for the customer.
Put implementation/onboarding wages in COGS — they deliver the initial service.
Put customer success in operating expenses, because the source describes them as a selling function focused on renewals and upselling more products.
Apply the same logic to a subscription ecommerce business: a team whose job is driving repeat purchases and upgrades is retention/acquisition spend, not cost of delivering the order.
Correcting this classification will usually lower reported gross margin and raise operating expense — do it deliberately, not by accident.
caveats: The line between support and success blurs in small teams; document the rationale for how you split shared staff.
This is the source's classification rule; confirm treatment with your accountant if investors or auditors rely on the numbers.

cards.title: Third-Party Revenue Share Is Marketing, Not COGS
cards.summary: Paying an external partner a share of revenue for promoting your product belongs in marketing/operating expense unless they help deliver the service.
cards.use_when: Recording affiliate, marketplace or channel-partner commissions for an ecommerce store to keep gross margin meaningful.
steps: Identify what the third party actually does. If they only market or promote your product and are not involved in delivering it, the payment is a marketing cost, not COGS.
Record that revenue share in operating/marketing expense rather than COGS.
Reserve COGS treatment for partners genuinely involved in service delivery (for example a delivery API or infrastructure provider in your product path).
Because affiliate and marketplace commissions are variable and tied to sales, keep them visible as a separate marketing line so you can still evaluate fully-loaded contribution per order.
Re-check contracts when a partner's role changes from promotion to fulfilment or delivery.
caveats: The source frames COGS as only about delivery of the service; some marketplaces may bundle delivery and promotion, so separate the fees in the contract where possible.

cards.title: Tie Server and Hosting Costs to Business Usage
cards.summary: Cloud costs (AWS/Azure) left unchecked rise quickly; reconcile them to customer or usage growth with engineering.
cards.use_when: Running a hosted or usage-based digital store, app or subscription platform where cloud spend is a major COGS line.
steps: Treat monthly AWS/Azure fees as COGS for a rented-server model (owned hardware instead flows in as depreciation).
Track cloud cost against usage or number of accounts so that adding a customer does not double your cost unnecessarily.
Build a per-customer or per-usage view of infrastructure cost so you can see whether economics improve or degrade as you scale.
Hold periodic meetings between finance and engineering to review how cost should move as the business grows — the source flags this as the practical control.
When onboarding a new enterprise account, tie the incremental infrastructure cost to that account so pricing reflects real delivery cost.
caveats: The source describes the meeting cadence as a practice to adopt, not a proven benchmark.
Cloud pricing and dashboards change; verify the current AWS/Azure cost tools before building reports.

cards.title: Waste Control: Expiry Rotation, Fire Sales and Inventory Controls
cards.summary: Reduce COGS leakage by moving near-expiry stock first, using fire sales to clear aged goods, logging stock in/out, and counting periodically.
cards.use_when: Managing perishable or seasonal inventory and shrink in an ecommerce warehouse or 3PL.
steps: Track expiration and obsolescence dates per SKU and ship stock with the nearest expiration first, before touching stock with a longer window.
When stock is very close to expiry, run a fire sale to move it quickly at much lower margin rather than losing it entirely.
Log inventory when it enters and when it leaves the warehouse, and run periodic physical counts — the source identifies missing outbound logging as the control gap that enables theft.
Investigate recurring count variances as a signal of shrink or process error, and feed the cost back into your COGS assumptions.
Use the same rotation logic for seasonal goods: move the oldest season first and discount aggressively before the next season lands.
caveats: Fire sales protect cash but depress margin; the source presents them as a last-resort recovery, not routine strategy.
Physical counting frequency depends on volume and risk.

cards.title: Correct COGS Gives a Trustworthy Gross Margin Signal
cards.summary: Accurate elements and timing of COGS produce the gross margin that informs unit economics and business decisions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly accounts before making product-line, pricing or discontinue decisions.
steps: Audit each COGS line for correct inclusion: goods-related costs in, selling and promotion costs out.
Audit timing: match cost to the period the sale occurs, not when the invoice arrived, for physical goods.
After corrections, recalculate gross margin and check whether it still supports the price, the acquisition cost and the overhead contribution.
Use the corrected margin to answer the operational question the source highlights: can you make more of this product, or should you discontinue and build something new?
Repeat the audit when the model changes — for example when you move from self-fulfilment to a 3PL, or from owned to rented infrastructure.
caveats: The source does not prescribe an audit cadence; monthly or quarterly review is a reasonable adaptation.
Correct accounting alone will not fix a product whose unit economics do not work.

20-FIN / finance and accounting Goes here. A breakdown of Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) tailored for finance leaders and business founders, comparing how COGS is calculated in Consumer Packaged Goods (CPG) versus Software as a Service (SaaS) business models. Not here. • Supply chain sourcing or negotiating factory prices -> 18-COG • Product pricing strategy and offer structuring -> 03-OFF

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a clear, foundational understanding of how COGS and Gross Margins differ between CPG and SaaS businesses, including common accounting misclassifications that distort valuations. modules: [FIN] topics: [COGS, SaaS accounting, CPG accounting, gross margin, financial valuation, unit economics, AWS server costs, freight classification] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. unit economics / how COGS determines the remaining capital available for marketing and R&D per unit sold; valuation / why venture capitalists and private equity firms obsess over gross margin (which is dictated by COGS) when valuing a business; CPG COGS / calculating tangible COGS using raw materials, direct labor on the manufacturing floor, factory overhead, freight-in, and packaging; SaaS COGS / calculating intangible COGS using server costs (AWS/Azure), third-party delivery APIs, customer support wages, and onboarding/implementation wages; accounting flow / how CPG inventory hits the balance sheet as an asset before flowing to the P&L as COGS upon sale, whereas many SaaS costs (like wages) hit the P&L immediately; gross margin expectations / expecting 20-40% gross margins for manufacturing/CPG versus 70-90% for SaaS; freight misclassification / the common accounting error of recording "freight-out" (shipping to customers) as COGS, when it should be recorded as a selling/operating expense; SaaS misclassifications / incorrectly recording Customer Success wages (which are sales/upsell functions) or third-party revenue shares as COGS instead of operating expenses.

Look for.

The Freight Classification Rule: The strict accounting rule that "freight-in" (bringing materials to the factory) is part of COGS, but "freight-out" (shipping the final product to the customer) is an operating/selling expense and should NOT be in COGS.

The Customer Success Misclassification: Noting that while Customer Support and Implementation wages belong in SaaS COGS, Customer Success teams (who handle upsells and renewals) are a sales function and belong in operating expenses.

Gross Margin Benchmarks: The rule of thumb that traditional CPG/manufacturing businesses operate at 20-40% gross margins, whereas SaaS businesses operate at 70-90% gross margins.

SaaS Server Depreciation: The explanation that if a company owns its physical servers, the cost enters COGS as depreciation over time, but most modern companies rent via AWS/Azure and log the monthly fee directly as COGS.

Skip. Plugs for the creator's "Controller Academy" website and generic requests to like/subscribe.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (fundamental accounting definitions and reporting rules). Volume. ~350 words.

In this video, we'll go over why CFOs obsess over COGS or cost of good sold. And the reason why this conversation is important to you as a finance leader or even a business founder is this can help guide the discussion that you have with auditors and investors. So, if this sounds good to you, let's dive right in. Hey everyone, this is Bill Hannah, your favorite financial controller, bringing about 20 years of experience in corporate accounting and finance leadership. and I teach my experience here in this YouTube channel as well as on my website, the Controller Academy, for which I'll leave a link down below. In today's video, we're discussing why CFOs obsess over COGS. But before jumping into the various elements of the video, I want to quickly address why CFOs spend a lot of time thinking about COGS. The first reason is going to be unit economics. So from each unit that we sell, say we sell something for $10, the COGS is going to determine how much money is left over that we can spend on marketing and research and development. So that's reason number one. Reason number two is valuation. Uh when VCs and private equity values a business, they think of revenue growth and gross margin. Gross margin is dependent on COGS. That's why it becomes a highly important thing for a valuation of a business. All right. So to structure today's video, we'll be talking about two main industries. The first one is going to be CBG or consumer package goods and the other one is SAS or software as a service because cost of goods sold is going to be different in these industries. So overall when we talk about CPG the cost of goods sold is going to be tangible. So the product is tangible. It's something that you can touch. So think of a company like Nike that manufactures sneakers and athletic attire. So their inventory is tangible, something that you can touch and therefore their cogs is going to be tangible. It's something that you can touch with the software as a service. An example of that is Salesforce. So Salesforce sells the platform of sales and marketing businessto business. So it's a B2B SAS business. In their case, their product is not tangible. So, it's a cloud-based product and most of the cogs that goes into it is going to be labor based, which is the salaries of the people who are supporting the delivery of that service. Okay, so let's go ahead and break that down. So, for a company that is CPG, let's say Nike, the COGS is going to be raw material plus direct labor plus overhead. raw material. If you're making a pair of sneakers, it's going to be uh rubber, uh leather, maybe laces. Uh direct labor is going to be the labor of the person who's standing on the manufacturing floor processing the actual manufacturing of the sneakers. The overhead is going to be the other costs such as the rent of the factory, uh depreciation of the factory if you own it, uh depreciation of the equipment, uh maintenance, utilities and things that uh keep the manufacturing operation running. Uh the second thing is going to be the freight in the cost to bring in the inventory uh and then packaging at the end when you make the pair of sneakers, you need to put it in a box and that is part of your cogs as well. Okay, so this is the breakdown for a CPG. What is about the breakdown for a SAS company? Uh these are the common costs that go into COGS. So the first one is server cost. So to deliver the service to your customers, you need to have a server and that server could be something physical that you own. So if you own an actual server, uh then the cost that goes here is going to be the depreciation over time of that server. Uh but most companies nowadays don't have their own physical server. We're talking about small businesses. uh what you do in this case is you go to AWS, Amazon Web Services or you go to Azure and uh lease or rent a server space and pay a monthly rent for that and that's going to be your server cost that goes here. Uh the second item that goes into cost is going to be tools to deliver the service. Um these are things like API or thirdparty tools that you need to have in place to be able to deliver that uh SAS uh product to your customers. Uh the third thing is going to be customer support wages. This is the wages that you pay uh to your customer support uh staff. Implementation wages. This is the salaries and the benefits that you pay to the team within your company that implements or on board the client uh with the new product that they just purchased. Okay. Let's spend some time talking about the recording and the timing of that recording for COGS. And for those of you who are accountants, it's really helpful to understand how information goes from data to populate the financial statements. And for that, I created an Excel file that actually helps you uh take a sample set of data and create financial statements from it. I'll leave a link down below for you to download that file. But for the recording of COGS for CPG, typically the information goes into the balance sheet. So when you create inventory that becomes an asset on the balance sheet and then that gets recorded to the P&L as COGS when when the inventory is sold when you make a sale right for a SAS business uh you also have a similar mechanic. So there is a flow from the balance sheet to the P&L and that has to do with your fixed asset. So a lot of times you have a fixed asset that relates to the actual delivery of the service which could be a computer cost, server cost and these are fixed assets that flows into COGS after that. But you also have a fair amount of COGS that gets recorded directly into COGS and these are things like customer support wages and implementation wages. And if this video is providing you with real value, don't forget to hit the like and subscribe button which will pay me back from my efforts that I'm doing here. Okay, so the next item is going to be gross margin. So typically with a CPG manufacturing based business, you have high cogs and low gross margin. Typically it's between 20 to 40%. Um so when I worked at a manufacturing company that made baby food products, uh the gross margin was about 30% and that's typical for that kind of business. With a SAS company, you typically have lower cogs in relation to revenue. you have lower COGS and you have high gross margin. So typically it's between 70 and 90% gross margin. So you might say maybe I should go into business here in SAS uh instead of going into a CPG product business. And the answer is yes. A SAS has higher gross margin, but in the end it's going to depend on the skill that you have. Maybe you have a killer idea for a CBG product that's going to have a very quick and high distribution and you'll have a small slice of the pie, but you're going to have a huge pie to get a small slice from. So, at the end, you win. Uh, but if of course if you have a really good idea for a SAS product, the gross margins are really appealing. Okay. Now, let's talk about the final point which is really most important is the common mistakes. What are the common mistakes that finance leaders and business founders make in relation to the cogs of the products? So the first thing is going to be waste. Uh the first item is going to be expired goods. So you need to keep tabs on the expiration and the obsolescence uh dates of your goods. Uh because if you're getting close to the expiration date, you should be moving the products with the near expiration first before you touch the products that have a longer expiration window or obsolescence window. Right?
